extracted.intended_audience: researchers and graduate students in differential and algebraic geometry (people studying K-stability and canonical Kähler metrics)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions and criteria for K-stability of a polarised variety (X,L), including the required structure of test configurations, Donaldson–Futaki invariants, norms, and alternative/related notions (toric, slope, filtration, Hilbert/Chow). Useful for checking or proving (semi-/poly-)stability and its relation to existence of Kähler–Einstein / cscK metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert–Mumford criterion (point stability analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Hilbert–Mumford criterion: for a point x in a projective variety X ⊂ CP^N with reductive group action G, test 1-parameter subgroups λ: C*→G and compute the weight μ(x,λ). x is semistable if μ(x,λ) ≤ 0 for all λ, stable if μ(x,λ) < 0 for all λ, and unstable if μ(x,λ) > 0 for some λ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finite-dimensional GIT criterion motivates K-stability: to test stability of a variety one should consider one-parameter deformations of the variety (test configurations). The page presents this as the analogue upon which K-stability is modelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test configuration (definition / admissible deformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A test configuration for a polarised variety (X,L) is a pair (𝒳,𝒟) where 𝒳 is a scheme with a flat morphism π:𝒳→C and 𝒟 is relatively ample for π, such that (1) for every t∈C the Hilbert polynomial of the fibre (𝒳_t,𝒟_t) equals the Hilbert polynomial P(k) of (X,L) (flatness ensures this), (2) there is a C* action on the family (𝒳,𝒟) covering the standard action on C, and (3) for any t∈C* the fibre (𝒳_t,𝒟_t) ≅ (X,L) as polarised varieties (i.e., the family is trivial away from 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page also defines special types: a product configuration if 𝒳 ≅ X×C, and a trivial configuration if the C* action is trivial on the X factor. Generic fibres are isomorphic to X while the central fibre may differ (possibly singular). Test configurations arise (and can be dominated) by blowups of X×C along C*-invariant ideals (flags of subschemes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight function and Hilbert polynomial expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: For a test configuration, the total weight w(k) of the induced C* action on H^0(𝒳_0,𝒟_0^k) and the Hilbert polynomial P(k)=dim H^0(X,L^k) admit asymptotic expansions for large k: P(k)=a_0 k^n + a_1 k^{n-1} + O(k^{n-2}) and w(k)=b_0 k^{n+1} + b_1 k^n + O(k^{n-1}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These coefficient expansions are the raw data used to form the Donaldson–Futaki invariant and other invariants (e.g., normalized weight w(k)/(kP(k)) expansion f_0 + f_1 k^{-1} + ...). The page notes these polynomial behaviours arise from equivariant Riemann–Roch and flatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Donaldson–Futaki invariant (weight / stability datum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Donaldson–Futaki invariant of a test configuration (𝒳,𝒟) is DF(𝒳,𝒟) = (b_0 a_1 - b_1 a_0) / a_0^2. Equivalently DF(𝒳,𝒟) = -f_1 where f_1 is the 1/k term in the expansion w(k)/(kP(k)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DF can be defined differentially (Ding–Tian) or algebraically (intersection-theoretic CM-weight after compactification over P^1); the DF invariant coincides with the CM-weight. It is invariant under replacing L by a positive power L^r, and can be expressed via Chow forms or hyperdiscriminants. In the toric setting DF can be written as 1/2 · 𝓛(f) = 1/2(∫_{∂P} f dσ − a ∫_P f dμ) for convex f on the moment polytope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norm of a test configuration (Székelyhidi norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a test configuration, let A_k be the infinitesimal generator of the C* action on H^0(X,L^k). Then Tr(A_k^2) has expansion Tr(A_k^2)=c_0 k^{n+2} + O(k^{n+1}). The norm is defined by ||(𝒳,𝒟)||^2 = c_0 − b_0^2 / a_0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The norm is used to exclude degenerate/trivial degenerations when defining K-stability: positivity of DF is required only for test configurations with positive norm in the K-stable condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: K-semistability / K-stability / K-polystability / K-unstability (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a polarised variety (X,L): K-semistable if μ(𝒳,𝒟) ≥ 0 (e.g., DF ≥ 0) for all test configurations. K-stable if μ(𝒳,𝒟) ≥ 0 for all test configurations and μ(𝒳,𝒟) > 0 whenever ||(𝒳,𝒟)|| > 0. K-polystable if K-semistable and whenever μ(𝒳,𝒟) = 0 the test configuration is a product configuration. K-unstable if not K-semistable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the algebraic stability notions that are conjecturally (and in many cases proven to be) equivalent to existence of canonical metrics (KE or cscK). The page emphasizes the need to exclude certain degenerate configurations (e.g., those of zero norm) and the refinement introduced by Li–Xu and Székelyhidi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yau–Tian–Donaldson conjecture (metric ↔ algebraic criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture / theorem statements: a Fano manifold X admits a Kähler–Einstein metric in c_1(X) iff (X,-K_X) is K-polystable; more generally a smooth polarised (X,L) admits a constant scalar curvature Kähler (cscK) metric in c_1(L) iff (X,L) is K-polystable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Fano case has been resolved (Chen–Donaldson–Sun, others). The page presents this as the principal motivation for K-stability: an algebraic criterion characterising existence of canonical Kähler metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Toric criterion (testing via convex functions on the moment polytope)
rubrics_metrics.description: For toric polarised varieties (X_P,L_P) one can test K-stability using toric test configurations described by convex functions f on the moment polytope P. The Donaldson–Futaki invariant is DF = (1/2) 𝓛(f) = (1/2)(∫_{∂P} f dσ − a ∫_P f dμ) and the norm is ||(𝒳,𝒟)|| = ||f − f̄||_{L^2} where f̄ is the average of f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For toric surfaces it suffices to test simple rational piecewise-linear convex functions (f = max(0,h) with rational affine h). The page gives an explicit example showing F_1 (first Hirzebruch surface) is K-unstable by computing these integrals for f(x,y)=x+y.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic Hilbert and Chow stability (GIT-based alternatives and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given r≫0 with L^r very ample, embed (X,L^r) in a Hilbert scheme and use Geometric Invariant Theory to define (asymptotic) Hilbert or Chow stability. Define Chow_r(X,L) = r b_0 / a_0 − w(r)/P(r). K-stability is the limit of Chow stability: DF = lim_{k→∞} Chow_{rk}(X,L^k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records implication relations: asymptotically Chow stable ⇒ asymptotically Hilbert stable ⇒ asymptotically Hilbert semistable ⇒ asymptotically Chow semistable ⇒ K-semistable. It notes it is unknown whether K-stability implies asymptotic Chow stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slope K-stability (testing by subschemes / deformation to the normal cone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the slope μ(X) = a_1 / a_0 from the Hilbert polynomial of X. For a subscheme Z ⊂ X, consider the Hilbert–Samuel polynomials χ(L^r ⊗ I_Z^{x r}) = a_0(x) r^n + a_1(x) r^{n-1} + ..., and define μ_c(I_Z) = (∫_0^c (a_1(x) + (a_0'(x)/2)) dx) / (∫_0^c a_0(x) dx) for c ∈ (0, ε(Z)]. The pair (X,L) is slope K-semistable if for all proper subschemes Z and all such c, μ_c(I_Z) ≤ μ(X) (with strict inequalities/extra conditions defining slope K-stability / polystability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slope K-stability arises from considering special test configurations given by the deformation to the normal cone (blow up of Z×{0}). Ross–Thomas showed K-semistability implies slope K-semistability, but the converse need not hold (flags of length >1 may be required). Use slope K-stability to identify K-unstable examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filtration K-stability (filtrations of the coordinate ring)
rubrics_metrics.description: A filtration χ of the coordinate ring R = ⊕_{k≥0} H^0(X,L^k) is a chain C = F_0 R ⊂ F_1 R ⊂ ... ⊂ R satisfying: multiplicativity ((F_i R)(F_j R) ⊂ F_{i+j} R), compatibility with grading (homogeneous pieces of f ∈ F_i R lie in F_i R), and exhaustion (∪_i F_i R = R). The Rees algebra Rees(χ) = ⊕_{i≥0} (F_i R) t^i ⊂ R[t] is finitely generated iff the filtration arises from a test configuration. Székelyhidi defines filtration K-stability using such filtrations (including limits of test configurations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filtration K-stability was introduced to capture destabilising degenerations that are limits of test configurations; finitely generated filtrations correspond exactly to test configurations (Witt Nyström), and arbitrary filtrations are limits of finitely generated ones. The page suggests replacing or refining K-stability by filtration K-stability to account for such limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test configurations via blow ups and flags of subschemes (construction / reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every test configuration is essentially obtained by blowing up X×C along a C*-invariant ideal I = I_0 + t I_1 + ... + t^{r-1} I_{r-1} + (t^r), which corresponds to a flag of subschemes Z_{r-1} ⊂ ... ⊂ Z_1 ⊂ Z_0 ⊂ X inside X×{0}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This structural description (due to Ross–Thomas and Mumford) allows reduction of general test configurations to blowups along flags; in length-one cases this yields the slope test configurations (deformation to the normal cone). It explains why flags of length >1 are necessary in general (slope alone is insufficient).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection-theoretic CM-weight expression
rubrics_metrics.description: After compactifying a test configuration over P^1, the CM-weight is defined by CM(𝒳,𝒟) = (1 / (2(n+1)·L^n)) (μ· n (Ḹ)^{n+1} + (n+1) K_{Ḹ/ P^1} · (Ḹ)^n) where μ = - (L^{n-1}·K_X) / L^n. The Donaldson–Futaki invariant coincides with the CM-weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides an intersection-theoretic/algebraic description of the DF invariant used in algebraic geometry (Tian's CM-weight approach). It is used in many algebraic verifications of stability and relates to Kähler geometry via equivalence with differential definitions.
